यथा रूपस्याऽऽलोकस्तथा रूपज्ञानं, विकारकारणं मनसो विषयान्तरम् । यथाऽग्निः पाक्यस्य । प्रत्ययकारणं धूमज्ञानमग्निज्ञानस्य । प्राप्तिकारणं योगाङ्गानुष्ठानं विवेकख्यातेः ।
वियोगकारणं तदेवाशुद्धेः । अन्यत्वकारणं यथा सुवर्णस्य सुवर्णकारः । एवमेकस्य स्त्रीप्रत्ययस्याविद्या मूढत्वे द्वेषो दुःखत्वे

मिन्द्रियद्वारा वा स्वतो वा विषयस्य संस्क्रियाऽभिव्यक्तिस्तस्याः कारणं यथा रूपस्याऽऽलोकः । विकारकारणं मनसो विषयान्तरम् । यथा हि कण्डोः समाहितमनसो वल्लकीविपञ्च्यमानपञ्चमस्वरश्रवणसमनन्तरमुन्मीलिताक्षस्य <gloss>१</gloss> स्वरूपलावण्ययौवनसंपन्नामप्सरसं प्रम्लोचामीक्षमाणस्य समाधिमपहाय तस्यां सक्तं मनो बभूवेति । अत्रैव निदर्शनमाह—यथाऽग्निः पाक्यस्य <gloss>२</gloss> तण्डुलादेः कठिनायवयवसंनिवेशस्य प्रशिथिलावयवसंयोगलक्षणस्य विकारस्य कारणम् । सत एव विषयस्य प्रत्ययकारणं धूमज्ञानमग्निज्ञानस्येति । ज्ञायत इति ज्ञानमग्निश्चासौ ज्ञानं चेत्यग्निज्ञानं तस्य । एतदुक्तं भवति—वर्तमानस्यैवाग्नेर्ज्ञेयस्य प्रत्ययकारणतया कारणमिति । औत्सर्गिकी निरपेक्षाणां कारणानां कार्यक्रिया प्राप्तिस्तस्याः कुतश्चिदपवादोऽप्राप्तिः । यथा निम्नोपसर्पणस्वभावानामपां प्रतिबन्धः सेतुना तथैहापि बुद्धिसत्त्वस्य सुखप्रकाशशीलस्य स्वाभाविकी सुखविवेकख्यातिजनकता प्राप्तिः । सा कुतश्चिद्धर्मात्तमसो वा प्रतिबन्धान्न भवति । धर्माद्योगाङ्गानुष्ठानाद्वा तदपनये तदप्रतिबद्धवृत्तिस्वभावत एव तज्जनकता तदाप्नोति । यथा वक्ष्यति—निमित्तमप्रयोजकं प्रकृतीनां वरणभेदस्तु ततः क्षेत्रिकवदिति ।

तदेवं विवेकख्यातिलक्षणकार्यापेक्षया प्राप्तिकारणमुक्तम् । अवान्तरकार्यापेक्षया तु तदेव वियोगकारणमित्याह—वियोगकारणमिति । अन्यत्वकारणमाह—अन्यत्वकारणं यथा सुवर्णकारः सुवर्णस्य, कटककुण्डलकेयूरादिभ्यो भिन्नाभिन्नस्य भेदविवक्षया कटकादिभिन्नस्याभेदविवक्षया कटकाद्यभिन्नस्य सुवर्णस्य कुण्डलादन्यत्वम् । तथा च कटककारी सुवर्णकारः कुण्डलादभिन्नसुवर्णादन्यत्कुर्वन्नन्यत्वकारणम् । अग्निरपि पाक्यस्यान्यत्वकारणं यद्यपि तथाऽपि धर्मिणो धर्मयोः पुलाकत्वतण्डुलत्वयोर्भेदाविवक्षया धर्मयोरुपजनापायेऽपि धर्म्यनुवर्तत इति न तस्यान्यत्वं शक्यं वक्तुमिति विकारमात्रकारणत्वमुक्तमिति न संकरः । न च संस्थानभेदो धर्मिणोऽन्यत्वकारणमिति व्याख्येयम् । सुवर्णकार इत्यस्यासंगतेः । बाह्यमन्यत्वकारणमुपन्यस्याऽऽध्यात्मिकमुदाहरति—एवमेकस्येति । अविद्या कमनीयेयं कन्यकेत्यादिज्ञानम् <gloss>४</gloss> । तन्मोहयोगात्त एव स्त्रीप्रत्ययो

As light is to form, so is knowledge of an object; it is the cause of the modification of the mind by an external object. As fire is to that which is being cooked. As the knowledge of smoke is the cause of the knowledge of fire. The practice of the limbs of Yoga is the cause of the attainment of discriminative knowledge.
That same [practice] is the cause of separation from impurity. The cause of distinctness is like the goldsmith in relation to gold. Thus, in relation to a single perception of a woman, <term>avidyā</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss> [leads to] infatuation, aversion [leads to] suffering.

...through the senses or by itself, the manifestation of the object through processing is its cause, just as light is to form. [It is] the cause of the modification of the mind by another object. For example, when a man whose mind is concentrated hears the fifth note played on a lute, his eyes open, <note>original: "१"</note> and seeing the nymph Pramlocā, who is endowed with beauty, luster, and youth, he abandons his <term>samādhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> and his mind becomes attached to her. Regarding this, it provides an example: As fire is the cause of the modification of that which is to be cooked, <note>original: "२"</note> such as rice, which is characterized by the loosening of the conjunction of its hard constituent parts. The knowledge of smoke is the cause of the perception of fire of an object that already exists. "Known" is knowledge, and that which is fire and is also knowledge is "fire-knowledge," of that. This is what is meant: the fire, which is the object of knowledge and is currently present, is the cause because it is the cause of the perception. The attainment of the action of an effect is the natural manifestation of causes that are not obstructed; the lack of attainment is the exception to this due to some cause. Just as a dam obstructs water, which has the nature of flowing downwards, so too here, for the <term>buddhi-sattva</term> <gloss>the essence of intelligence</gloss>, which has the nature of pleasure and illumination, the generation of discriminative knowledge of happiness is natural attainment. That does not occur due to some obstruction caused by merit or darkness. By the removal of that through the practice of the limbs of Yoga, the generation of that [knowledge] is attained by the very nature of an unobstructed flow. As it will say: "The cause is not the activator of the natures, but the removal of the obstruction occurs; it is like the farmer."

Thus, the cause of attainment is stated with respect to the effect characterized by discriminative knowledge. With respect to the intermediate effect, it is the cause of separation, which it states: "cause of separation." It states the cause of distinctness: "The cause of distinctness is like a goldsmith in relation to gold." Gold, which is different from a bracelet, earring, etc., when one wishes to express difference, is different from the bracelet; when one wishes to express non-difference, it is non-different from the bracelet. Thus, a goldsmith, a maker of bracelets, by making something different from the gold that is not different from the earring, is the cause of distinctness. Although fire is also the cause of distinctness for that which is to be cooked, still, because one does not wish to express the difference between <term>pulāka</term> <gloss>shriveled grain</gloss> and <term>taṇḍula</term> <gloss>husked rice</gloss>, which are two properties of the underlying substance, the substance persists even when the properties arise and pass away; thus, it cannot be said to be distinct, and so it is stated to be the cause of the modification alone, hence there is no confusion. And it should not be interpreted that the difference in form is the cause of the distinctness of the underlying substance; [otherwise] the reference to the "goldsmith" would be incoherent. Having posited the external cause of distinctness, it gives an example of an internal one: "Thus, for one..." <term>Avidyā</term> is the knowledge that "this maiden is desirable," etc. <note>original: "४"</note> Due to the association with that delusion, that very perception of the woman...

XXXIII. Concerning Imaginary Time, we judge the same as we do concerning Imaginary Space: that beyond the intrinsic durations of things, which provide the foundations for various relations of distance and proximity, it is in reality nothing at all.

XXXIV. Finally, duration is either created or uncreated. The uncreated is proper to GOD alone and is called Eternity. It is defined by Boethius: *The simultaneous and perfect possession of interminable life.* Of created duration, one kind is temporary and the other is perpetual. The temporary is that which has both a beginning and an end. The perpetual is that which, at the least, has no end; such as the duration of Angels and of the rational soul, which is also called the Aevum <note>a state of existence between time and eternity</note> and is commonly defined as: *The interminable permanence of a thing in an existence once received.*

### ON QUANTITY.

XXXV. Aristotle describes "the quantum" <note>the quantitative</note> here in book 5, text 18: *That which is divisible into things that are present, where each one or every one is some "one thing," and this "something" is apt to be.* That is to say (as Father Suarez interprets it), those things which, by their own nature, are each apt of themselves to remain as a certain whole, separated from others. And it is indeed divisible, according to the force of quantity, in the same way—namely, by physical and natural divisibility—by the power of which one body naturally expels another, or expels its parts from the place they previously occupied.

XXXVI. It is an opinion, as Father Suarez says, sufficiently common among the Thomists that the primary formal effect of quantity is the distinction of integral parts; so that without quantity, neither prime matter nor any other material entity would have any integral parts. Father Vasquez, among our own, followed the Thomists in his *Commentary on the Summa*, vol. 3, part 3, disputation 190, from number 20. But this is against: 1. For just as every thing is a being through itself, so it is "one" through itself, and consequently divided and distinct from any other thing. 2. Because otherwise one would have to proceed to infinity. For if one thing is distinct from another by a third entity, then it would have to be distinguished from that third by a fourth, and so on to infinity. 3. Because matter is presupposed to quantity with its entire entity. Therefore, it cannot receive parts from it; since a whole is nothing other than all its parts, if it is presupposed with its entire entity, it must also be presupposed with its parts. Therefore, the primary formal effect of quantity cannot consist in the distinction of parts.

As light is to form, so is the perception of form; it is the cause of modification, another object for the mind. As fire is to that which is to be cooked. The cause of perception is the knowledge of smoke for the knowledge of fire. The cause of attainment is the practice of the limbs of Yoga for discriminative discernment.
The cause of separation is that same practice for impurity. The cause of differentiation is, for example, a goldsmith for gold. Thus, in the case of a single perception of a woman, ignorance is the cause of delusion, while aversion is the cause of suffering.

<column-break/>

Through the senses or by itself, the manifestation of the transformation of an object—its cause is like light for form. The cause of modification is another object for the mind. For instance, consider the man whose mind was composed, yet who, immediately upon hearing the fifth note played on a lute <note>original: "vallakī"</note>, opened his eyes and gazed upon the nymph Pramlocā, who was endowed with beauty and youth; he abandoned his concentration (<term>samādhi</term>) and his mind became attached to her. Here, the text provides an illustration: **"As fire is to that which is to be cooked,"** <note>referring to rice, etc., which possesses a structure of hard components; fire is the cause of its modification, defined as the loosening of the combination of its parts.</note> So too, the knowledge of smoke is the cause of the perception of fire, for an object that already exists. "Knowledge" (<term>jñāna</term>) means that which is known; "fire" is the known and "knowledge" is the perception, so this refers to the knowledge of fire. This is what is meant: the fire, which is already present as an object to be known, serves as the cause because it is the object that produces the perception. By nature, the causal efficacy of causes that are not obstructed results in the attainment of their effect; the exception to this, where attainment does not occur, is due to some hindrance. Just as the flow of water, which naturally tends to move downward, is blocked by a dam, here too, the intellect (<term>buddhi-sattva</term>), which is of the nature of happiness and luminosity, naturally tends to generate discriminative discernment. That generation does not occur due to some obstruction, such as demerit (<term>dharma</term>) or darkness (<term>tamas</term>). Upon the removal of that obstruction through merit or the practice of the limbs of Yoga, the intellect attains the capacity to generate that discernment, purely by virtue of its own unobstructed nature. As the text will say: "The cause is not the activator of the creative sources; rather, it is the removal of the barrier, like a farmer."

Thus, the "cause of attainment" has been stated with regard to the effect characterized as discriminative discernment. With regard to an intermediate effect, it says that the same is the "cause of separation." It states the "cause of differentiation": just as a goldsmith is to gold. Gold, which is distinct or non-distinct from bracelets, necklaces, and armlets, differs from a pendant depending on whether one wishes to focus on the distinction of form or the non-distinction of substance. Thus, the goldsmith, who creates something else from the gold—which is non-distinct from the pendant—is the cause of differentiation. Although fire is also the cause of differentiation for that which is being cooked, one cannot say there is differentiation in the substance, because when the two attributes (the state of being rice grains or rice mush) are not regarded as distinct, the substance persists even if its attributes appear and disappear. Therefore, it is stated to be merely the cause of modification, so there is no conflation of categories. It should not be explained that a change in configuration is the cause of a change in the substance, for that would make the example of the "goldsmith" incoherent. Having posited an external cause of differentiation, it illustrates an internal one: **"Thus, in the case of a single..."** Ignorance is the perception, such as "This woman is desirable," etc. Due to the association with delusion, that same perception of a woman...
